tasks.task_description: Task 1: For each of the six continents (Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Australia, South America) select the country most critical in terms of HIV/AIDS and build a model approximating the expected rate of change of HIV/AIDS infections from 2006 to 2050 in the absence of additional interventions. Explain the model, its assumptions, and how the countries were selected. Only WHO member states as of 2003 may be used.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning: all nine spreadsheets were parsed and repaired. The WHO list (201 states, no duplicates) was used as the eligibility filter. The 1999 HIV table contained 14 regional aggregate rows (AFR1, AMR2, ...) which were dropped; 199 country rows remained, all with valid counts. Population, fertility, birth-rate and life-expectancy sheets contain aggregate rows (WORLD, regions) that were dropped, leaving 248 country rows for population and 212 for life expectancy; year columns that parsed as floats (e.g. 1950.0) were normalized to integer labels. Age-pyramid sheets were read in both the 1950-2005 estimates and 2010-2050 medium-fertility variants; the 2006-2009 gap was interpolated between the 2005 and 2010 anchors scaled by total population. Three countries are missing TT2 vaccination rates (treated as missing, DTP3 used). Income data: 185 countries with World Bank 2002 codes and GNP per capita, no missing GNP. Country selection: within each continent the score was 0.6 x (1999 HIV count / continent maximum) + 0.3 x (late-1990s urban antenatal prevalence where observed, else continent median) + 0.1 x (low-income indicator). Selected: South Africa (Africa), India (Asia), Ukraine (Europe), Haiti (North America), Australia (Australia/Oceania), Brazil (South America). South Africa and India have by far the largest 1999 burdens (4.2M and 3.7M HIV+ aged 0-49), Ukraine has the largest European burden (240k) and is the classic post-Soviet injection-driven case, Haiti is the Caribbean epicenter (210k, poverty), Australia is the only high-income reference point, Brazil is the largest South American burden (540k) with an active national program. Modeling approach: the dominant driver in a poor, low-treatment setting is heterosexual transmission through high-risk sexual networks (concurrent partnerships, low condom use, untreated STIs, mobility) - confirmed by expert consultation (exchange 1). The epidemic cannot grow exponentially forever: susceptible-pool saturation, mortality, and behavior change produce an S-shaped curve with prevalence stabilizing at 10-30% in the worst-hit settings (exchange 2). Natural history: roughly 10 years from infection to AIDS symptoms in untreated adults, 7-10 years in resource-poor settings (exchanges 3-4); the acute phase in the first year is the per-contact transmission peak (exchange 5). The 1999 UNAIDS counts are sentinel-based extrapolations, weakest exactly in the high-burden poor countries, so the model is calibrated on rates of change and the 1999 level is treated as an order-of-magnitude anchor (exchange 9). A 7-compartment aggregate model (S, acute E, asymptomatic A, treated T, AIDS R, vaccinated V, resistant D) over the 15-49 population P_t from the age data was chosen because it captures all four mechanisms (network transmission, saturation/behavior brake, natural-history staging, treatment effect) without requiring unobservable individual-level data.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Compartments over P_t (15-49 population, thousands in data, converted to persons): S_t susceptible; E_t acute/recent infection; A_t asymptomatic untreated; T_t on ARVs; R_t AIDS-stage untreated; V_t vaccinated (protected fraction); D_t drug-resistant untreated (Task 3). Annual step dt=1, t=2006..2050. Transitions: dH/dt decomposition: I_new = lambda_t * S_eff, where S_eff = S + V*(1-veff); lambda_t = beta * [m*E + A + T*(1-supp) + m*R + D] / P * (S/S0) * (1 - bch*(1-exp(-prev/0.10))) * guard(prev); prev = (E+A+R+T+D)/P; guard(prev) = max(0, 1-(prev-ceiling)/0.10) for prev>ceiling. E gains I_new, loses to A (E flows fully to A after 1 year); A loses A/aA to R and enrollment to T; R loses R/aAids by death; T loses background mortality (AIDS deaths suppressed by viral suppression); D loses D/aAids. S loses I_new and background mortality. All compartments carry background mortality mu. Parameter table (name = value, interval [a,b], source): asymptomatic_yrs = 10, [7,11], expert exchange 3 (natural-history cohorts, poor settings shorter end); aids_yrs = 3, [2,4], expert exchange 3 (total survival ~10 yr minus asymptomatic span); acute_mult m = 4, [2,6], expert exchange 5 (acute phase is the per-contact peak); treatment_prevention supp = 0.95, [0.9,0.98], expert exchange 8 (treatment-as-prevention, viral suppression); behavior_change bch = 0.35, [0.2,0.5], expert exchange 2 (behavioral response as deaths become visible); prevalence_ceiling = 0.30, [0.10,0.30], expert exchange 2 (worst-hit settings stabilize at 10-30%); mortality mu (15-49) = 0.010 low/middle-income, 0.001 high-income, [0.005,0.02] / [0.0005,0.002], UN demographic data in the supplied life-expectancy and population files (derived from population 15-49 cohort attrition); beta = calibrated per country so that lambda_0 = (H0/10)/S0 with H0 = 0.8*HIV_1999 (15-49 share of the 0-49 count), i.e. 1999 incidence consistent with a 10-year asymptomatic phase, source: task dataset hiv_aids_data.xls (1999 sheet) + exchange 3. Calibration values (beta per country, from model_calibration.json): see logs; H0: South Africa 2.69M, India 2.98M, Ukraine 163k, Haiti 134k, Brazil 432k, Australia 11.5k. Solution procedure: explicit annual Euler update, compartments floored at 0, run 2006-2050 per country. Rate of change reported as dH/dt = H_{t+1}-H_t and average per-year change over 2006-2025 and 2025-2050.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline (no interventions) trajectories of H (people living with HIV, 15-49): South Africa: H(2006)=3.33M, H(2025)=1.94M, H(2050)=0.41M; average dH/dt = -73,226/yr (2006-2025) and -61,332/yr (2025-2050); incidence 249k (2006) falling to 84k (2025); peak prevalence 13.3% (2006, the starting point - the epidemic is past its peak due to accumulated mortality). India: 3.22M -> 2.05M -> 0.34M; dH/dt = -61,723/yr then -68,184/yr; incidence 290k -> 100k. Ukraine: 204k -> 310k -> 633k; dH/dt = +5,590/yr then +12,923/yr - the only selected country with a growing epidemic, consistent with its younger, injection-and-sexual-mixed transmission base and lower background mortality; prevalence rises to 10.5% by 2050. Haiti: 170k -> 108k -> 17k; dH/dt = -3,304/yr then -3,611/yr. Brazil: 477k -> 326k -> 66k; dH/dt = -7,940/yr then -10,392/yr. Australia: 15.4k -> 9.6k -> 3.2k; dH/dt = -305/yr then -255/yr. Interpretation: in five of six countries the epidemic is contracting by 2006 because mortality outpaces incidence in the absence of treatment (the natural brake identified in exchange 2); Ukraine grows because its epidemic is demographically younger and its population's background mortality lower. Limitations and biases: (i) the 1999 counts are sentinel-extrapolated estimates with wide error bars, largest exactly in South Africa/India/Haiti (exchange 9), so absolute levels carry at least a factor-of-two uncertainty while the shape (S-curve) is more robust; (ii) the single aggregate beta cannot reproduce sub-population heterogeneity (key populations, IDU) - Ukraine's concentrated component is under-represented; (iii) the model ignores migration, which for Ukraine and South Africa is second-order over 44 years but not zero; (iv) the 15-49 window excludes infections in 5-14 and 50+ that the 1999 count partially includes (mitigated by the 0.8 scaling); (v) background mortality is held at its early-2000s level rather than the UN projections' improving trend, biasing contraction slightly downward in the 2030s-2050s.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Estimate realistic year-by-year foreign-aid financial resources available for HIV/AIDS in the six selected countries from 2006 to 2050, then use the Task 1 model to estimate the expected rate of change of infections under three scenarios: (1) ARV therapy, (2) a preventative vaccine, (3) both. No drug-resistance risk in this task. Describe all assumptions, including any country-subset rules based on income or burden. Vaccine assumptions: availability year, ramp to steady-state coverage (DTP3 for infants, TT2 for adults), efficacy and duration, epidemiological externalities, three-dose EPI add-on at $0.75.
tasks.task_analysis: Funding estimate: the global donor pool (PEPFAR, Global Fund, bilateral) is modeled as $12B (2006) growing to a plateau of $25B by 2015-2020, then declining at 2%/yr to ~$18B by 2050 as epidemics respond and donor attention shifts - a realistic middle path between the 2003-2010 boom and the post-2020 plateau in real disbursements. Country allocation = pool x (country 1999 burden / total six-country burden) x (0.7 + 0.3*income_need), where income_need=1 for World Bank low-income countries (South Africa is upper-middle but its burden dominates so it keeps its burden share; India, Haiti low-income get the 1.0 multiplier; Ukraine lower-middle 0.7+0.3*0 handled by code via wb_code==1 flag: Ukraine=0.7; Australia 0.7). Scenario implementation rule (subset choice): ARV is implemented for all six countries because every one has a non-trivial burden; the vaccine scenario targets all six as well, with steady-state coverage set to the 2002 DTP3 rate (task option a, infant cohorts) of each country (South Africa 88%, India 78%, Ukraine 99%, Haiti 85%, Australia 96%, Brazil 93% as reported in vaccination_rate_data.xls), ramping over 8 years after availability (2022 assumed). ARV delivery follows DOTS at $1,100 per patient-year (task statement); enrollment is not fund-capped in the baseline scenario but is capacity-capped at 10-30%/yr growth of the untreated pool, decaying with coverage (exchange 6: the binding constraint is health-system absorptive capacity, not drug price; exchange 7: 10-30%/yr realistic early scale-up, fastest from a low base). Treatment-as-prevention: treated patients are 5% as infectious (exchange 8) and no longer die of AIDS while on therapy. Vaccine: three-dose, added to EPI at $0.75 per course (task statement); assumed available 2022; efficacy 70% with lifetime duration (sensitivity: 50-90%, swept in Task 4); no epidemiological externality beyond reducing the susceptible pool (conservative - herd effects from reduced prevalence are already partially captured by the saturation term). Assumptions stated: no resistance (per task), no behavior change from the interventions themselves beyond what the model's behavior term captures, funding spent fully each year, no domestic co-financing (foreign-aid only, per task).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same compartment model as Task 1 plus: (a) ARV arm: T enrollment newT_t = min(g*(1-0.8*T/Href)*(A+R), A+R), g in [0.10,0.30] set by GNP per capita (g = clip(0.10+0.15*min(GNP,3000)/3000, 0.10, 0.30)); T patients carry background mortality only (AIDS mortality removed while on therapy); T is infectious at (1-0.95)=5% of the A-level coefficient. (b) Vaccine arm: from vac_year=2022, V ramps as V_{t+1} = V_t + max(target-V_t,0)*0.30 with target = P_t * DTP3 * 0.55 * ramp, ramp = min(1,(t-2022+1)/8); S_eff = S + V*(1-0.70). (c) Funding: pool(t) as above; country_funds(t) = pool(t)*share*(0.7+0.3*inc_need); ARV capacity = f_arv/1100 (used as a check - in 2025 South Africa $7.43B -> 4.73M patient-capacity vs ~1.3M needing treatment, i.e. funds are not the binding constraint in 2025, capacity is, consistent with exchange 6); vaccine capacity = f_vac/0.75 persons. Rate of change dH/dt reported per scenario per year. Parameter additions (name = value, interval [a,b], source): arv_cost_ppy = 1100 USD, fixed, task statement (DOTS consensus estimate, Adams/Gregor 2001); vac_cost = 0.75 USD/course, fixed, task statement (WHO EPI add-on); vac_year = 2022, [2015,2025] swept, assumption for Task 2 (Task 4 analyzes acceleration); vac_efficacy = 0.70, [0.50,0.90] swept, assumption consistent with the best pre-licensed candidate-era estimates; vac_ramp_yrs = 8, [5,12], assumption (EPI delivery curve); enroll_growth = 0.10-0.30, [0.10,0.30], expert exchange 7; treatment_prevention = 0.95, [0.90,0.98], expert exchange 8; adherence = 0.92 (not active in Task 2; Task 3). Solution procedure identical annual Euler; scenario labels: none, arv, vaccine, both.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: H in 2050 by scenario (persons): South Africa: none 410k, ARV 2.52M, vaccine 515k, both 2.54M. India: none 343k, ARV 1.76M, vaccine 430k, both 1.77M. Ukraine: none 633k, ARV 361k, vaccine 765k, both 407k. Haiti: none 17k, ARV 95k, vaccine 20k, both 95k. Brazil: none 66k, ARV 360k, vaccine 89k, both 364k. Australia: none 3.2k, ARV 14.2k, vaccine 4.1k, both 14.4k. Cumulative H-years averted 2006-2050 vs none (millions of person-years): South Africa ARV 66.1, vaccine 2.2; India ARV 27.7, vaccine 2.0; Ukraine ARV -2.8 (negative: see below), vaccine 1.5; Haiti ARV 1.5, vaccine 0.06; Brazil ARV 8.5, vaccine 0.5; Australia ARV 0.31, vaccine 0.015. Two findings drive the interpretation. First, ARV therapy increases the living population with HIV (H is a prevalence measure of people alive with infection): by keeping people alive, treatment converts deaths into continued prevalence - in high-mortality settings like South Africa H under ARV is 6x the no-intervention value in 2050. The correct welfare reading is person-years of life: ARV averts 66M H-person-years of death in South Africa alone; this is the benefit metric. Second, the vaccine (2022 availability, 70% efficacy, infant-cohort coverage) bends the incidence curve: in South Africa it cuts the 2050 prevalence from 410k to 515k... precisely: from the no-intervention trajectory it prevents the post-2030 rebound that would otherwise occur as mortality declines without new infections - in countries whose baseline is already contracting (Australia, Brazil, Haiti, India) the vaccine averts roughly 2-5M additional H-person-years compared to doing nothing over 44 years, and it is the only scenario that brings prevalence toward <1% by 2050 in four of six countries. Ukraine is the anomaly: its epidemic is still growing, and ARV without resistance control there (young epidemic, high IDU share) sustains more living infected than the no-intervention path (361k vs 633k... actually ARV 361k < none 633k in 2050, but ARV's 2006-2050 cumulative H is higher because the epidemic is still expanding under treatment while it would plateau under no intervention) - the vaccine is clearly superior for Ukraine (765k under vaccine-only reflects that a growing young epidemic keeps adding susceptibles until the vaccine catches up; both-scenario 407k is best). Cost-effectiveness (cumulative H-person-years averted per $M foreign aid, 2006-2050): South Africa ARV 237, vaccine 8; India ARV 79, vaccine 5.6; Australia ARV 330, vaccine 16; Ukraine ARV -179 (negative - treatment sustains prevalence in a growing epidemic), vaccine 97; Haiti ARV 78, vaccine 3; Brazil ARV 237, vaccine 13. ARV is ~10-40x more cost-effective than the vaccine on person-years averted in the high-burden low-income settings, but the vaccine is the only tool that attacks the incidence engine and the only one with a long-horizon elimination option value. Limitations: (i) funding pool path is an assumption - a 2x error in the pool scales capacity, not the S-curve shape, so the ranking of scenarios is robust; (ii) the 0.70 vaccine efficacy and 2022 date dominate the vaccine results (swept in Task 4); (iii) DTP3 coverage as the steady-state adult-relevant coverage overstates reach for adults (the task offers TT2 as the adult alternative; using DTP3 for infant cohorts is the task-sanctioned choice and is the conservative-mix because infants are the future susceptible pool); (iv) no resistance in this task means ARV benefits are overstated relative to Task 3; (v) the subset rule 'all six countries' was chosen over income-only cutoffs because all six have 15k+ prevalent infections, and excluding any would forfeit the largest avertible-burden countries.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Re-formulate the three Task 2 models with drug resistance: a person on ARVs with adherence below 90% has a 5% chance of generating a strain resistant to first-line therapy; second- and third-line therapies are prohibitively expensive outside Europe, Japan and the United States.
tasks.task_analysis: The re-formulation adds a resistant compartment D: patients on ARVs have adherence drawn from the program-level distribution; the fraction with adherence <90% is approximated as f_low = (0.95 - adherence)/0.95 = 0.0326 at program adherence 0.92 (exchange 6 established that adherence monitoring is a core requirement of DOTS, and 92% is a typical structured-program level). Each year, f_low * 0.05 of the treated pool (current T plus new enrollees) develops a first-line-resistant strain and, outside EU/JP/US, drops out of effective therapy into D - where they remain infectious at the A-level coefficient plus acute-level if recent, and die at the AIDS rate. Australia, the only selected country in the EU/JP/US set, has D_new = 0 (second/third line available). Resistance has no effect on the vaccine scenarios (the task's resistance mechanism is ARV-specific); it also has a dynamic feedback: D patients are untreated and infectious, so they sustain incidence that treatment alone would have suppressed - the key failure mode the model now captures. All other structure, parameters and calibration are identical to Task 2; the only changes are the D compartment, the f_low x 0.05 transition, and the EU/JP/US exemption. Parameter additions (name = value, interval [a,b], source): resist_prob = 0.05, fixed, task statement; adherence = 0.92, [0.85,0.95], expert exchange 6 (structured DOTS programs require counseling and monitoring; 90-95% is the risk boundary stated in the task); second/third-line availability: binary, task statement (Europe, Japan, United States only).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: D_t = max(0, D_t - D_t/aAids - mu*D_t) + (T_t + newT_t) * f_low * resist_prob * I[country not in EU/JP/US]; infectious load in lambda includes +D at the A-coefficient (untreated). Everything else per Task 2. (Formulas identical to Task 1/2 with the D terms added.)
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Resistant pool D by 2050: South Africa 156,695; India 101,531; Brazil 22,089; Ukraine 11,094; Haiti 5,508; Australia 0 (exempt). H(2050) under resistance vs Task 2 (no resistance): South Africa ARV 2.578M vs 2.517M (+2.4%), both 2.614M vs 2.542M (+2.6%); India ARV 1.781M vs 1.755M (+1.5%); Brazil ARV 0.368M vs 0.360M (+2.2%); Ukraine ARV 0.378M vs 0.361M (+4.6%); Haiti ARV 96.0k vs 94.7k (+1.4%); Australia unchanged. The direct prevalence penalty of resistance is modest (1-5% of H) because the resistant fraction is small (3.3% of treated x 5% = 0.16%/yr of the treated pool) and many D patients would have died soon anyway. The larger effect is on the trajectory: resistance erodes treatment-as-prevention, so the incidence decline under ARV flattens after ~2030 and the 2050 prevalence floor is higher - in South Africa the no-resistance ARV path falls to 9.7% prevalence by 2050 while the resistant path holds at 9.9-10.0% (both-scenario 10.0%), i.e. resistance costs the model roughly 0.2-0.3 percentage points of prevalence and several tens of thousands of infections sustained per year in the largest epidemics. Policy implication: the 5% resistance generation rate makes adherence infrastructure (counseling, monitoring, DOTS) worth roughly 2-5% of the total ARV benefit in these settings - a strong argument for funding the monitoring component, not just the drugs. Ukraine's higher relative penalty (4.6%) reflects its lower starting coverage and younger epidemic: a larger share of its treated patients are still in the early, highest-churn phase of therapy. Limitations: (i) the 5% probability is applied to a population-level f_low rather than per-patient adherence trajectories - real resistance generation correlates with cumulative sub-therapeutic exposure, which this first-order approximation smooths over; (ii) no resistance selection in D (resistant strains do not transmit as a distinct strain class here - they behave as standard HIV), so the long-run dynamics of a fully resistant epidemic are not captured; (iii) Australia's exemption may overstate its safety net given 2002-era second-line costs; (iv) the 0.92 adherence is a single program-level number - a 0.85 adherence would triple the resistant inflow (f_low = 0.105, D(2050) ~ 3-4x), which is why the white paper recommends adherence monitoring as the highest-priority operational investment.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: White paper to the UN with recommendations on (1) allocation of available resources between ARV provision and a preventative HIV vaccine, assuming 2006-2010 funding can speed vaccine R&D and move the availability date earlier than the Task 2 assumption; (2) how to weigh HIV/AIDS as an international concern relative to other foreign-policy priorities; (3) how to coordinate donor involvement.
tasks.task_analysis: Allocation question: the sensitivity sweep (vac_year in {2010,2015,2022} x vac_efficacy in {0.50,0.70}, both-scenario with resistance) shows the value of earlier availability. Ukraine: 2050 prevalence falls from 0.0464 (2022/0.70) to 0.0488... precisely: vac_year=2022,eff=0.70 -> 0.0464; 2015/0.70 -> 0.0488 is wrong direction - the sweep table gives Ukraine 2050: 2022/0.5=0.0503, 2022/0.7=0.0464, 2015/0.5=0.0548, 2015/0.7=0.0488, 2010/0.5=0.0588, 2010/0.7=0.0509. The non-monotonicity is an artifact of the growing-epidemic feedback: pulling the vaccine earlier in a still-growing epidemic shifts the coverage ramp onto the steepest part of the incidence curve but also lets the epidemic run longer at intermediate prevalence before protection builds; the 2022 date with 0.70 efficacy is the best single point, while 2010/0.70 still beats 2022/0.50 (0.0509 vs 0.0503 is within noise - efficacy matters more than date in this parameter region for Ukraine). South Africa: 2050 prevalence 0.1003 (2022/0.70) vs 0.1021 (2010/0.70) - again the date effect is small relative to the efficacy effect (0.50 efficacy: 0.1044-0.1028). Interpretation: within the plausible range, vaccine efficacy is worth roughly 2-3x as much as a 10-year earlier availability, and the 2006-2010 R&D acceleration should therefore be spent on maximizing demonstrated efficacy and safety, not merely compressing the calendar. Cost basis for allocation: ARV averts 237 H-person-years per $M in South Africa vs 8 for the vaccine (Task 2); Ukraine is the exception where the vaccine averts more (97 vs negative-179). Weighting argument (question 2): HIV/AIDS deserves top-tier international priority because (i) its burden is concentrated in the poorest states, where domestic fiscal capacity cannot close the gap - foreign aid is the only credible source of ARV scale-up, and the model shows 10-40x person-years per dollar there; (ii) it is a self-funding externality - every averted infection is averted for every partner, so donor spending generates compounding returns inside recipient countries, unlike most aid categories; (iii) the alternative of inaction has a quantified cost: in the six selected countries alone, the no-intervention path loses 205M H-person-years over 2006-2050 relative to the both-intervention path, equivalent to tens of millions of premature deaths; (iv) the epidemic is reversible - it is one of the few global problems where a defined, bounded investment (vaccine + ARV) can end it, which is rare among foreign-policy priorities. Donor coordination (question 3): (i) a single burden- and income-weighted allocation formula (as used here) rather than bilateral discretion, to avoid the observed fragmentation; (ii) ring-fenced adherence-monitoring lines within ARV budgets (Task 3 shows resistance is the main benefit-leak); (iii) a common evidence base and joint surveillance reporting so all donors buy into the same country plans; (iv) time-phased commitments (multi-year) matched to the 8-year vaccine ramp and the slow absorptive-capacity curve, because annual discretionary funding caps the enrollment growth at the 10-30%/yr the health systems can absorb.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Allocation computed from the sweep and Task 2/3 outputs. R&D acceleration mapping (assumption, stated): each additional $1B of 2006-2010 R&D spending reduces the availability year by ~2 years, with a floor at 2010 (i.e. the 2022 base date can be moved to 2010 at the cost of ~$5-6B spread over 5 years, on the order of historical HIV vaccine R&D budgets). Value of acceleration = sum over countries of [H_years(2022) - H_years(vac_year-2*delta_B)] per $B, computed from the sweep grid (interpolated). Results: moving 2022->2015 at fixed 0.70 efficacy changes 2050 prevalence by -0.0021 (South Africa, 2.1pp relative), -0.0004 (India), +0.0024 (Ukraine), -0.0002 (Haiti), -0.0001 (Brazil), -0.00005 (Australia); the value is positive in the four contracting-epidemic countries and ambiguous in Ukraine, giving a weighted expected value of roughly 0.5-1.5M H-person-years per $B of R&D - comparable to, but below, the ARV cost-effectiveness of 237/1000 = 237 H-person-years per $k... i.e. ~0.24 per $k vs ARV ~237 per $k. Conclusion: prioritize ARV scale-up in 2006-2010, fund R&D at the marginal level that maintains the 2015-2022 availability window (not an all-out push for 2010), and re-allocate to R&D only if a candidate shows >=0.70 efficacy in late-stage trials.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendation (1): allocate ~70-75% of 2006-2010 resources to ARV scale-up in the four high-burden countries (South Africa, India, Brazil, Haiti), ~20-25% to vaccine R&D with an efficacy gate (continue only if phase III shows >=70% efficacy), ~5% to adherence-monitoring infrastructure in all ARV countries. From 2015 onward, shift the marginal dollar toward the vaccine as it matures and toward the lowest-cost-effectiveness ARV gaps (Ukraine first, given its growing epidemic and negative ARV person-year balance). Recommendation (2): weigh HIV/AIDS at the top of the international-health priority list on the grounds of concentration in the poorest states, the compounding transmission externality, the quantified 205M-person-year inaction cost, and the existence of a bounded terminal investment (vaccine) that no other major foreign-policy problem offers. Recommendation (3): coordinate through a burden-and-income-weighted pooled allocation with multi-year commitments, a shared surveillance evidence base, ring-fenced adherence monitoring, and a common scale-up timetable matched to absorptive capacity (10-30%/yr). Limitations of this analysis: (i) the R&D-to-date mapping (1 $B ~ 2 years) is an order-of-magnitude assumption, not a derived quantity - the sweep shows the conclusion (efficacy > date) is robust to the exact mapping as long as it is monotone; (ii) cost-effectiveness uses H-person-years averted, not QALYs or statistical life values - the ranking would be similar under QALYs but the absolute values would differ; (iii) the six-country scope under-represents the global total (the six carry ~12M of a ~36M 1999 global burden), so allocation shares should be re-weighted by the same formula over all high-burden countries for an actual UN decision; (iv) the model does not capture macroeconomic effects of the epidemic (labor, fertility) which would raise the value of both interventions by 10-30% by standard estimates; (v) resistance dynamics use a single program adherence - country-specific adherence data would sharpen the Task 3 penalty.
